item.title: C# Reflection: How to Determine Generic List Item Type Dynamically
item.description:
“C# Reflection: How to Determine Generic List Item Type Dynamically”

When working with dynamic data structures, serialization, or complex reflection scenarios in C#, a common requirement is determining the specific type argument (T) held within a generic collection like List<T> or IEnumerable<T> when the collection variable is not strongly typed in the source code (e.g., it’s treated as object or a non-generic interface).

This article presents several established methods and alternative approaches for retrieving this inner type dynamically using reflection.

item.title: C# Reflection: Retrieving Property Values Based on Custom Attributes
item.description:
“C# Reflection: Retrieving Property Values Based on Custom Attributes”

How does one effectively utilize C# reflection to inspect properties of a type, identify those adorned with specific custom attributes (like an AuthorAttribute), and subsequently extract the data encapsulated within those attributes? Several robust methods exist, ranging from iterative loops to concise LINQ expressions.

Method 1: Iterative Property Scanning with Attribute Casting

This approach involves explicitly retrieving all properties of a given type, then iterating through each property’s custom attributes, checking the attribute type, and populating a dictionary with the resulting property name and attribute value.

item.title: C# Techniques to Automatically Get Variable Name in Method Calls
item.description:
“C# Techniques to Automatically Get Variable Name in Method Calls”

Programmers often desire to automatically capture the name of a variable supplied as an argument to a method, particularly for generating informative error messages during validation or logging. Since C# local variable names are generally erased during compilation or not directly accessible at runtime without specific mechanisms, how can we achieve this automatic capture? Several creative solutions, ranging from modern C# features to intricate reflection hacks, have been proposed.

item.title: C# Type.GetType Null Resolution Strategies When Assembly Context is Missing
item.description:
“C# Type.GetType Null Resolution Strategies When Assembly Context is Missing”

When employing reflection in C#, obtaining a Type object from a string representation of its name is a common operation. However, the standard Type.GetType(string typeName) method has specific limitations: it typically only successfully resolves types residing within mscorlib.dll or the currently executing assembly. If your target type exists in a referenced assembly, direct resolution often yields null.

What are the established methods and workarounds for retrieving a Type object when only its fully qualified name or partial name is known, especially when dealing with types in external DLLs or nested structures?

item.description:

item.title: Executing Uncompiled Java Source Code Programmatically in Java
item.description:
“Executing Uncompiled Java Source Code Programmatically in Java”

How does one execute Java code that exists only as source text (e.g., a String or file content) without relying on an external compilation step? This scenario demands leveraging the Java Development Kit (JDK) features directly within the running application. The key lies in utilizing the Java Compiler API (javax.tools).

Method 1: Direct Compilation and Loading via javax.tools.JavaCompiler

To process source code not yet compiled into bytecode, you must first invoke the JDK’s compiler programmatically. This requires the local machine to have the JDK installed, as the JRE alone is typically insufficient for accessing the compiler tools.

item.title: Go Struct Tags Explained: Usage with Reflection and Common Packages
item.description:
“Go Struct Tags Explained: Usage with Reflection and Common Packages”

In the Go programming language, struct tags are special string literals appended to a field declaration within a struct. They provide a mechanism to attach arbitrary metadata to that field, information that is typically leveraged by external packages or custom logic accessed through the reflect package at runtime.

Core Purpose and Convention of Struct Tags

A struct tag’s primary function is to embed meta-information about how a struct field should be transformed when encoded or decoded into different formats (like JSON, XML, or database records) or how it should be stored/retrieved.

item.title: Java Generics: How to Instantiate Type T Without Explicit Constructor Reference
item.description:
“Java Generics: How to Instantiate Type T Without Explicit Constructor Reference”

A frequent challenge when working with Java generics is the inability to directly instantiate the type parameter T within a generic class or method due to type erasure at runtime. How can one effectively create an instance of T when only its generic type declaration is available? This post details several established solutions to work around this limitation.

Alternative Approaches for Constructing Generic Instances

The core issue stems from Java’s design choice to use type erasure for generics. This means that at runtime, the specific type T is often lost. Several patterns exist to reintroduce this type information or provide an alternative means of object creation.

item.title: Java Methods: How to Retrieve the Name of the Currently Executing Method
item.description:
“Java Methods: How to Retrieve the Name of the Currently Executing Method”

In Java development, particularly during debugging, logging, or building utility classes, dynamically determining the name of the method currently executing can be extremely valuable. This requirement presents several technical avenues, each with distinct trade-offs regarding performance, version compatibility, and robustness against VM optimizations.

How can one reliably capture the executing method’s name across different Java versions and execution contexts? We survey several accepted solutions and weigh their practical implications.

item.title: Java Reflection for Retrieving Local Variable Names at Runtime
item.description:
“Java Reflection for Retrieving Local Variable Names at Runtime”

How can one retrieve the names of local variables or method parameters within a running Java program, especially when standard java.lang.reflect APIs seem insufficient? This query delves into the limitations and alternative approaches for accessing this metadata, which is typically stripped out during compilation for optimization or obfuscation.

The Challenge: Accessing Local Variable Names via Standard Reflection

The core difficulty lies in the fact that Java Virtual Machine (JVM) specification generally does not mandate the retention of local variable names in the deployed bytecode, except under specific conditions.

Since the standard Java Classloader API does not natively offer an “enumerate all classes” function—primarily due to the immense performance overhead of scanning potentially thousands of classes—developers rely on specialized libraries or framework utilities.

item.title: Dynamically Creating Generic C# Instances with Reflection
item.description:
“Dynamically Creating Generic C# Instances with Reflection”

When working with C# generics, a common challenge arises when you need to instantiate a generic type whose specific type argument is not known until runtime. This scenario typically occurs when the type information is loaded from configuration files, external assemblies, or user input. In such cases, the compiler cannot resolve the generic type, and a direct instantiation is not possible. The primary mechanism to overcome this is by leveraging .NET’s reflection capabilities.

item.title: Java Reflection: Accessing Private Fields Safely and Effectively
item.description:
“Java Reflection: Accessing Private Fields Safely and Effectively”

When developing in Java, you might encounter situations where you need to access private fields of a class. This is typically an encapsulation violation, but there are scenarios, especially in testing or framework development, where it becomes necessary. Java’s reflection API provides a powerful mechanism to achieve this, though it comes with its own set of considerations and potential pitfalls. This article delves into various methods for accessing private fields using reflection and explores alternative strategies.

item.title: How to Find All Classes in a Java Package Programmatically
item.description:
“How to Find All Classes in a Java Package Programmatically”

Discovering all classes within a specific Java package at runtime can be a valuable task for various programming needs, such as plugin architectures, dependency injection frameworks, or dynamic class loading. While Java’s class loading mechanism is dynamic and doesn’t natively expose a direct API for this, several approaches leverage filesystem operations, JAR file introspection, and third-party libraries.

The Challenge: Dynamic Class Loading

Java’s class loaders are designed to load classes on demand. They are not mandated to provide a mechanism to list all classes they can provide; they simply respond to requests for specific classes and throw an exception if a class cannot be found. This dynamic nature means directly querying a class loader for all classes in a package isn’t straightforward.

item.title: C# Reflection: Accessing Object Properties Dynamically with String Paths
item.description:
How can I access an object’s property dynamically using a string that represents its name or a path to a nested property in C#?

When working with objects in C#, you often need to access properties based on a string name or a hierarchical path. This is particularly useful when dealing with configurations, serialization, or when the property you need to access isn’t known until runtime. Reflection in .NET provides powerful mechanisms to achieve this. Here, we examine several effective methods and their nuances for dynamic property retrieval.
